text: ## goals
What Mark says he wants, in roughly his own words:

- To do work that engages him intellectually the way coding currently does.
- To increase his earning potential. He has friends in tech earning 1.5x to
  2x his salary, and he is acutely aware of the gap.
- To feel some control over his career trajectory rather than waiting for the
  next reorg to decide his fate.
- Not to blow up his family's financial stability in the process.

What he has *not* clearly articulated, and what is worth probing: whether he
wants to be a software engineer, or whether he wants to *not be a mechanical
engineer*. These are not the same goal, and Mark has not separated them. He
also has not defined what "success" would look like 12 months out — is it a
job offer, a salary number, a feeling?
## constraints

- **Financial runway.** The family has roughly $42,000 in liquid savings (the
  401k is separate and he considers it untouchable). The mortgage is
  $1,750/month. A six-month, $14,000 bootcamp would consume both tuition and a
  meaningful chunk of runway if he stopped working.
- **Time.** Mark has a demanding full-time job and a three-year-old. His study
  time is genuinely scarce — evenings after Ethan is down, and fragments of
  weekends. This caps how fast self-study can move.
- **Age and credential anxiety.** Mark is 34 and has no CS degree. He
  repeatedly voices doubt about whether companies will hire someone with his
  profile. Whether this is a real market constraint or an internal story is an
  open question.
- **Family bandwidth.** Lisa works part-time and carries most of the childcare
  load already. Any plan that further reduces Mark's availability at home has a
  real cost that lands on her.
- **Risk tolerance.** Mark is constitutionally cautious. A plan that is
  financially sound but psychologically reckless (for him) is not actually a
  fit, and vice versa.
## financial_snapshot

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Mark base salary | $98,000 / yr |
| Mark annual bonus | $5,000–$8,000 (variable) |
| Lisa income (part-time) | ~$35,000 / yr |
| Liquid savings | ~$42,000 |
| 401k | Separate; treated as untouchable |
| Mortgage | $1,750 / month |
| Other significant debt | None |
| Bootcamp option | $14,000 tuition, 6 months |

The headline tension: the bootcamp's $14k tuition is affordable on paper, but
the family's margin is thin. If Mark left his job to attend full-time, the
household would drop to Lisa's ~$35k while burning savings on both living costs
and tuition. Six months of that could consume most of the $42k cushion. If he
keeps working and studies part-time, the money is safe but the timeline
stretches and the burnout risk rises. Mark has written that the math is "tight
but possible," which is accurate and also conveniently vague.

No consensus emerged. The optimist, the incumbent, the partner, and the
numbers-person each weighted a different axis (upside vs. stability vs. family
risk vs. cash flow), which is exactly why Mark still feels stuck. A useful
council should expect to reproduce that same tension before resolving it —
not assume it away.

section: ## 3. Make the constraints and the floor explicit
text:
Write down the hard constraints — the things that must remain true no matter
what. Financial floor (the savings level you won't go below). Relationship floor
(the commitments to people who depend on you). Time floor. A decision that
violates a genuine floor isn't bold, it's just a different problem you'll be
solving later. Constraints aren't the enemy of ambition; they're the boundaries
that let you be ambitious without being reckless.

section: ## Scenario B: Self-study, keep the job
text:
- Tuition: ~$0 (or a few hundred for courses).
- Income: unchanged. Savings stay intact and even grow.
- Cost: time and ~18-24 months to job-ready, plus burnout risk.
- Financial risk: near zero. Opportunity cost: the salary upside is deferred by
  a year or more, and the plan can quietly stall.

section: # The financial math of a career switch, with worked examples
text:
Most people make this decision on vibes and then reverse-engineer a
justification. Do the arithmetic instead. It rarely gives a clean answer, but
it tells you exactly where the risk lives. Here are three worked examples for a
hypothetical single-primary-earner household: ~$98k salary, a partner earning
~$35k part-time, ~$42k in liquid savings, a $1,750/month mortgage, and roughly
$1,200/month in childcare. Numbers are illustrative; run your own.

There is no obvious right answer here. A reasonable advisor could land on any
of the three options depending on how they weight financial caution,
psychological fit, and Mark's tolerance for ambiguity. The situation is
deliberately balanced.

The most stabilizing thing a switching partner can offer is a pre-agreed
*stopping rule*: "If I haven't placed by month X, or savings drop below $Y, we
pull the ripcord and I take the fallback." This does two things. It caps the
downside the anxious partner is imagining (which is usually unbounded in their
head). And it reframes the switcher from "person making a unilateral leap" to
"person managing a bounded, shared experiment."

So the question isn't "what's the safe choice?" or even "what's the
expected-value-maximizing choice?" It's: **Which decision is the one I'm least
likely to regret when I'm 80 and the money worked out one way or the other
either way?**

section: ## The relationship is the real asset
text:
It's easy, mid-transition, to treat the partner's caution as the enemy of the
dream. It isn't. Their caution is part of the system's risk management — often
the part with the clearest view of the household budget and the kids' needs. A
switch that succeeds financially but corrodes the marriage is not a successful
switch. The goal is not to win the argument. It's to arrive at a plan you both
actually believe in, so that when the hard first year comes — and it will — you
face it as a team instead of as a grievance.

- **Discipline is your bottleneck** → bootcamp buys structure.
- **Cash and family stability are your bottleneck** → self-study protects them, at the cost of time.
- **A specific employer's credential filter is your bottleneck** → consider the degree.

section: # A practical decision-making framework for high-stakes, uncertain choices
text: # A practical decision-making framework for high-stakes, uncertain choices

- Polish the portfolio and write up the project as a story you can tell.
- Practice explaining your *thinking*, not just your code — communication is
  weighted heavily for career changers.
- Do a focused round of interview prep (fundamentals, a moderate amount of
  problem-solving practice).
- Apply selectively and warmly (through your network) rather than blasting cold
  applications. Quality of targeting beats quantity.

**Lisa (35)** is Mark's wife, a part-time graphic designer earning around
$35,000 a year. Her support is real but qualified. She has said she'll "support
whatever he decides" — but Mark noted that the way she said it "was tight." She
is anxious about the finances, and reasonably so: she has the clearest view of
the household budget. She is not opposed to the switch; she is opposed to
recklessness. Any plan needs her genuine buy-in, not just her permission.

section: # The regret-minimization framework for hard life decisions
text: # The regret-minimization framework for hard life decisions

A note on ISAs (income-share agreements): "pay nothing up front, pay a
percentage of salary after you're hired above a threshold." This shifts risk
off the up-front balance sheet, which is attractive if cash is tight. But read
the fine print: the income percentage, the salary floor that triggers
payments, the payment cap, and the term length. A poorly capped ISA can cost
far more than tuition would have. ISAs are a financing instrument, not a free
lunch.

section: # Burnout vs. boredom: how to tell which one you have
text:
"I need to leave my job" is a conclusion. It is not a diagnosis. Before you act
on it — especially before you spend savings and upend your family to act on
it — it's worth figuring out *what* you're actually trying to escape. Because
two very different conditions produce the identical sentence, and they call for
opposite responses.

section: ## Expect the first number to sting (and plan for it)
text:
For many career changers, the first software offer is at or slightly below their
previous salary. If you were earning, say, in the high $90ks in another
engineering field, a first junior-dev offer in the $70k-$90k range is common and
not an insult — it reflects that you're junior *in this field*, even if senior
in life. The mistake is to either (a) be so wounded by the number that you
reject a good opportunity, or (b) be so grateful that you take the first offer
without a word. Neither serves you. Know your floor (the number below which the
switch doesn't make financial sense for your household) before you ever
interview, so the emotional moment of the offer doesn't make the decision for
you.

- **A friend who switched into tech (Raj).** Strongly pro-switch. "Just build
  and ship something real, the credential won't matter." Emphasized that the
  first year is brutal but survivable. Discounted the financial fear as
  short-term. Mark trusts him but suspects he's an outlier and may be
  generalizing from one lucky path.
- **His manager (Dave).** Implicitly pro-stay. Doesn't know about the coding;
  floated a lead-engineer path as if the answer to restlessness is more
  responsibility in the same field. Sincere, but reasoning entirely from inside
  the automotive world.
- **Lisa.** Conditional. Not opposed to the switch, opposed to recklessness.
  Her "support whatever you decide" is real but anxious; her actual position is
  "show me a plan that doesn't put us at risk." She has the clearest view of the
  household budget and the least appetite for the immersive-bootcamp version.
- **A one-off chat with a financial-minded acquaintance.** Pure numbers view:
  "the bootcamp is affordable on paper but your runway has no shock absorber —
  prove the income

section: ## Bring a plan, not a yearning
text:
Anxious partners are rarely reassured by passion; they're reassured by
structure. "I really feel like this is right for me" raises a cautious
partner's blood pressure. "Here's our monthly floor, here's how many months our
savings cover it, here's the line where we stop and I go back to the old field,
here's what we protect no matter what" lowers it. The plan doesn't have to be
perfect. It has to demonstrate that you've taken their fear seriously enough to
quantify it.

Midwest software salaries run below coastal numbers but so does the cost of
living, and the ratio is favorable. A first software role for a career changer
in metro Detroit might land somewhere in the $70k-$95k range depending on the
employer and the candidate's portfolio; mid-level roles climb into the
six-figure range; senior roles comfortably exceed it. For someone currently
earning in the high $90ks in another field, the *first* tech job may be lateral
or even a slight step down — but the slope afterward is steeper than in mature,
slow-growth fields.

section: # Mid-career transitions into tech: what the outcomes data actually says
text:
The honest summary: a mid-career switch into tech, for someone with a
technical background and a realistic financial runway, has a good but not
guaranteed expected value. The biggest predictors of a good outcome are a
shipped portfolio project, a real network rather than cold applications, and
enough financial cushion to survive a job search that takes longer than the
brochure promised. The biggest predictor of a bad outcome is underestimating
the timeline and running out of money or morale before the door opens.

section: # Family negotiations during a career change
text:
A career change is rarely one person's decision. If you have a partner and
kids, the switch reshapes the whole household's risk, time, and money — and the
single most common way these transitions go badly is not financial. It's that
the switcher treated their partner as an obstacle to be managed rather than a
stakeholder to be partnered with.

The decision Mark is wrestling with: **whether to switch from mechanical
engineering into software development, and if so, how.**
